title: How people read it
hookLine: it takes around ninety minutes; many read one ashtpadi a day
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 1, salok: I bow to the Guru
last: SUKHMANI — RESTING IN THE MIDDLE OF IT.

lines: A LONG BANI, A SHORT MORNING.
THE ANSWER IS IN THE STRUCTURE.
cards: Sukhmani is long. Read aloud at an unhurried pace, it fills a good stretch of a morning. So how does anyone with a job, children and a commute read it at all?
A grandmother up before dawn may read the whole of it, every day. A nurse on night shifts may not have that much quiet time in a week. Both can call Sukhmani their bani.
The answer isn't a trick. It's in how the text was built, eight stanzas at a time.

teach.b: Sukhmani is made of twenty-four ashtpadis. Asht is eight; pad is a stanza or verse. So an ashtpadi is an eight-stanza section.

Each opens with a short salok, two lines that set the theme, and then the eight stanzas unfold it. Twenty-four times eight is one hundred ninety-two stanzas in all. That structure is a gift to a busy person.
An ashtpadi is a complete thought, with a beginning, a middle and an end. You can read one in a few minutes and close the book having heard something whole. So people read Sukhmani in many ways.
Some read all of it every day, often early in the morning.

teach.h: ALL AT ONCE, OR ONE A DAY.
teach.b: Some read it through once a week.
Families and groups sometimes split it up, a few ashtpadis each, so that together they complete it. And some read one ashtpadi a day, so the whole bani comes round in twenty-four days.
Sikh tradition doesn't set one required pace for Sukhmani. What matters, in the bani's own words, is that the Name rests in the mind.
A rushed reading of all twenty-four isn't the goal; an attentive reading of one is a real reading.
That's the pace we'll take here: one ashtpadi at a time, its salok first, then a few days with its stanzas, then a day for living it.

how: Some Sikhs read the whole of Sukhmani Sahib daily or weekly; others read one ashtpadi a day, and families and groups sometimes divide the twenty-four ashtpadis among themselves to complete it together.

games.why: each ashtpadi is a complete thought, and some Sikhs read one at a time; attention matters more than speed.

practice: Think about your actual week, not an ideal one, and find a quiet ten minutes: Sunday before anyone's up, a lunch break in the car, the bus home.
Picture yourself there, reading eight stanzas slowly, then let the plan go and just breathe, as if that slot had already arrived. If you pray, say Waheguru once.
